tip: 'Ten' isn't a typo for 'tiene' – a few common verbs chop the 'tú' command to one syllable: 'ten', 'pon', 'sal'. 'Ten cuidado' is literally 'have care'.
'Sé paciente' = be patient: this 'sé' is the command of 'ser', spelled like 'sé' (I know); the accent separates both from 'se'.
'Di' wears two hats: the command 'tell!' from 'decir', and 'I gave', the past of 'dar'. 'Di la verdad' commands; 'ayer di las gracias' reports. Context decides.
Why 'está delicioso', not 'es'? Taste is a right-now verdict: 'está' reports how the dish hits your tongue tonight. 'Es delicioso' would rate the recipe in general.
'Para ser marzo' = 'considering it's March'. 'Para' + 'ser' sets a benchmark to judge against – the 'calor' is only remarkable by March standards.
You don't 'be' hungry in Spanish – you have it: 'tengo hambre', literally 'I have hunger'. Same club: 'tengo sed', 'tengo frío', 'tengo miedo' (thirst, cold, fear).
'Habrá' is 'hay' sent to the future – and like 'hay', it never pluralizes: 'habrá tiempo', 'habrá problemas'. One frozen singular form, however many things will exist.
English sneaks 'would' into if-clauses; Spanish never does. After 'si' it's 'estuviera', never 'estaría' – past subjunctive in the if, conditional ('iría') in the result.
'Cuya' agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: the male 'profesor' still gets 'cuya' because 'clase' is feminine. English 'whose' never changes shape.
Nobody used up the soap – it just ended: 'se ha acabado'. That 'se' makes it happen by itself, Spanish's built-in no-blame move for empty jars and dead batteries.
'Carro' is a car in Mexico and most of Latin America – in Spain it's a cart, and Spaniards drive a 'coche'. The same 'préstamo' would buy very different wheels in Madrid.
'Estará' isn't a prediction here – Spanish uses the future tense for guesses: 'dónde estará' = 'where can he possibly be?' Wondering aloud, not forecasting.
No 'si' in sight: 'de no haber sido por' = 'had it not been for'. 'De' + infinitive squeezes a whole if-clause into a phrase with no conjugated verb – compact, formal, very written-Spanish.
'Pregunta por María' doesn't order her like a menu item – 'preguntar por' means asking after someone. Requesting things is 'pedir'; people take 'preguntar por'.
'Me gustaría' = I would like, the conditional of 'gustar' for polite wishes. More polite than 'quiero'.
That '-id' ending marks the 'vosotros' command, Spain's informal plural: 'venid' = 'come, you all'. Latin America skips 'vosotros' and would say 'vengan' instead.
'Vamos a pedir' can mean 'we're going to order' – but launching a sentence with it usually means 'let's order!' Same phrase covers both plans and proposals.
'¿Le importaría...?' literally asks 'would it matter to you?' – Spanish's white-glove request, a notch above '¿podría?' Use it on strangers you're about to inconvenience.
'When you're older' feels like fact in English; Spanish treats unarrived time as unreal: 'cuando seas', not 'cuando eres'. Future-pointing 'cuando' takes subjunctive.
Two 'meets' in Spanish: 'nos encontramos' = we met up (a rendezvous – from 'encontrar', 'find'); 'conocer' is only for meeting someone for the first time.
'¿Le importaría...?' = Would you mind...? A very formal polite request using the conditional of 'importar'.
Careful answering '¿Te importaría...?': it literally asks 'would it bother you?', so 'sí' = 'yes, I'd mind' – a refusal! To agree to 'revisar', say 'claro' or 'no, en absoluto'.
No one's predicting the future here: Spanish future tense doubles as wondering aloud. '¿Quién será?' = 'I wonder who that is' – 'será' guesses, it doesn't forecast.
English uses plain present for future 'when' (when they grow up); Spanish flags the not-yet-real with subjunctive: 'cuando crezcan', never 'cuando crecen'.
'Quería que' + past subjunctive: 'quería que lo supieras' (I wanted you to know). A past wish plus 'que' takes the past subjunctive.
'No pude' isn't just 'couldn't' – the preterite means you hit the wall in that moment: I tried to answer and failed. Ongoing inability would be 'no podía'.
'Yo que tú' is literally 'I that you' – a whole if-I-were-you clause squeezed into three words. It always fires the conditional: 'no aceptaría'.
English strands prepositions ('the people I work with'); Spanish forbids it. 'Con' moves up front and 'que' takes an article: 'las personas con las que trabajo'.
Never translate 'embarrassed' as 'embarazada' – that means pregnant! The safe word is the one this card uses: 'avergonzado', from 'vergüenza' (shame).
'Del que' = of/about which: 'el tema del que hablamos'. It contracts 'de' + 'el' + 'que'.
